quote: Leave in the first hour, or make a plan to leave in the third week.
what_it_means: Everyone leaves at once. That is the whole of it. A road carries a certain number of cars an hour and no more. The southbound carriageway held for about ninety minutes on the first morning. Then it stopped being a road and became a long thin car park with families sitting in it. It never moved again. The first hour is empty because nobody has decided yet. The third week is empty because the cars have been left where they died and walked away from. In between is the worst place in England. Raghunathan walked out of her department at twenty past nine, against every instinct she had been trained into. She was past the ring road before the first ambulance failed to arrive.
how_to_use_it: The first hour is empty because nobody knows anything, and that includes you. She drove north for forty minutes towards a town the news had not reached, which was already gone, and she had to turn round. She lost the hour and she lived through losing it. That is the only reason this rule is at the front of a book instead of cut into a stone. Anybody moving in the first hour is moving on rumour at fifty miles an hour. The third week is slower, colder, hungrier and far more honest. If you have any way of holding out for it, hold out for it.

quote: Whatever you are locking out is in the building with you.
what_it_means: Okon cleared eleven premises in two days. In nine of them the doors had been made fast from the inside. By people who had shut the problem in with themselves and then gone to sleep. Turning takes hours. Somebody bitten on Tuesday afternoon is a colleague at nine, quiet at midnight and a catastrophe at four. The lock is on the wrong side of the question. Before you seal a room, count the people in it. Account for every one of them out loud. Look at the arms of anybody who says they are fine.
how_to_use_it: It turns you into a man who checks the arms of strangers, and that is a difficult thing to stop being. Okon searched a family of four at the Hunslet checkpoint on day nine, found nothing, and waved them through. He searched them again on day eleven, because by then he could not not do it. The father broke his cheekbone and took the checkpoint's food. I do not blame him. Suspicion is a tool with a very short handle. This rule is for a room you are about to seal. It has no business anywhere else.

quote: Fill the bath. Then fill everything else. Then sit down and think.
what_it_means: The towers are fed by gravity, so water keeps arriving for hours after the pumps have stopped, at a pressure that falls all afternoon. Then one time you turn the tap and it coughs. A bath is eighty litres. A cistern is nine. An older house has a tank in the loft with another two hundred in it that most people never think about. The order in the rule is the clever part: filling things needs no attention, so you can do your thinking while the taps run. Winslow filled the bath, four buckets, the kettle and two wheelie bins she dragged in over the kitchen lino. Only then did she get out a pencil.
how_to_use_it: Eighty litres weighs eighty kilos and you cannot carry a bath. There is a particular death that comes from having done something sensible on the first morning. It looks like a person standing in a well provisioned kitchen in June, unable to think of a reason to walk out of it. Winslow left hers on day thirty-one with a rucksack and a hand cart, and abandoned every drop. Fill the bath. Then do not let the bath make your decisions.

quote: What is on your feet when it starts is what you have got.
what_it_means: You are not going home. That is the part people took three weeks to believe. Tait believed it on the second morning. He had spent nineteen years walking off hills with people who had made exactly one bad footwear decision that day. Feet are the first thing to fail and the hardest to repair. He kept a tally through the first spring of the people he found who could not go on. It comes out at eleven in walking boots and sixty-four in something else. Look down. That is your whole vehicle now.
how_to_use_it: It became a superstition. Men who had got out in good boots would not take them off. By the second month there was rot in the county that had nothing to do with anybody being bitten. Boots come off at night. The other failure is Tait's own. Good boots made him confident. Confidence took him over the tops in April with weather coming. Mountain rescue is a thing that requires there to be a mountain rescue.

quote: Fifteen minutes of packing, then out, whatever is still on the table.
what_it_means: Packing expands to fill whatever time you give it, and the time you have is never what you think. Vrba loaded his car in fifteen minutes. He had loaded vehicles for a living for twenty-two years and knew the thing nobody else knows. It is not the carrying that takes the time. It is the choosing. A timer removes the choosing. He set the alarm on his phone, filled the boot, and drove off at eleven minutes past with the tailgate still up.
how_to_use_it: Fifteen minutes gets you the obvious, and the obvious is tins. Go through the notebooks and the same three things are left on the table in house after house: documents, medicine, and somebody's glasses. You can eat another man's tins. You cannot borrow his eyes. Vrba got out with four hundred tins and without his daughter's inhaler. He went back for it on day four, which is a thing this book tells you twice never to do. He came back with the inhaler. That is one of two occasions in eleven hundred notebooks where going back worked. It is in here so that you know how rare it is. Not so that you copy it.

quote: Down. Always down.
what_it_means: Height feels like safety and is not, because height is only safety if you can get off it whenever you choose. The lifts went in the first week. That leaves one staircase, and they climb stairs, badly and slowly and without ever getting bored. A tower block is a chimney with a single exit and four hundred people in it. Prentice had spent his working life at altitude on somebody else's building. He had a rigger's instinct about the way down being the part you plan first. He went down on the first afternoon, walked out of Little London, and is alive.
how_to_use_it: Down is where the water goes, and the smoke, and the crowd. Down is the street, and the street in the first week was the drift. The eleventh floor of Prentice's own block held out until the first week of May, on rainwater and a tank. Four of those people are alive too. This is the first place in the book where two good rules point opposite ways. Height traps you slowly and the ground kills you quickly. Which of those you would rather have is a real question with no general answer. Anybody who gives you one has not read enough notebooks.

quote: Nobody who is more than one street away.
what_it_means: It is arithmetic and it is not pleasant. Every retrieval costs you the journey out, the search, the argument on the doorstep and the journey back. Each of those is exposure. Exposure in the first week compounds. Hatherleigh had spent eleven years moving materiel. He wrote the rule at half past ten on the first morning, before he had seen one of them, on the back of a delivery note. It is the most hated sentence in this book. It is also, in the individual case, correct, and I have never found a set of numbers that says otherwise.
how_to_use_it: He went back for nobody. That included his brother in Armley, four streets off, and he was right, and it has eaten him alive for four years. Then there is the group problem. People will not follow a man they believe would not come for them. Hatherleigh's second group lost eleven of nineteen in the autumn. Not to anything that bit them. To nine people walking off in the night because of a rule pinned to a wall. A policy that is correct for one person can be fatal for twenty. Chapter eight is about that and about nothing else.

quote: Their blood will not kill you. Their spit will.
what_it_means: This is the single most useful sentence in the manual and the county had it backwards for the best part of a year. It passes in saliva, into blood, by a bite. Errai worked it out on the third day, from the pattern of who turned and who did not. Everybody bitten, and nobody else. That included two men who had spent a morning up to their elbows taking one apart. Blood on unbroken skin is nothing. Blood on your coat is nothing. Knowing that is the difference between two groups. One can clear a doorway. The other burns its own clothes and starves in a clean house.
how_to_use_it: It is true and it has a hole in it. Blood in an open cut, blood in an eye, blood in a mouth. Errai lost his assistant. She was splashed across the face cutting one down from a fence, and she had a torn cuticle on the hand she wiped herself with. There is no version of that sentence that would have saved her. Say the longer one. Their blood will not kill you through skin that is whole. You will not know which of your skin is whole until you check. So check.

quote: Off at the meter, and do the neighbours while you are out.
what_it_means: Fire took more of this city than they did. Nobody argues about that any more. A hob left on. A pilot light. A gas main under a house nobody is watching, and no brigade. A terrace burns as one long building, with party walls that were never meant to be the last line. Threlfall walked the length of Cross Flatts with a meter key on the second morning and shut off forty-one houses. Including his own. Including the four he had to break into. It took him ninety minutes and it is the reason that street is still standing.
how_to_use_it: Ninety minutes in the open on day two, alone, in daylight, is a fair description of how most of the dead in this book died. He got away with it. Then there is what he built. A street with no gas is a street with no cooking and no heat. By November people were burning furniture in the front rooms of houses that were beautifully safe from gas. Three of them went up anyway. He solved the fire of March and bought the fire of December, which is a trade, and worth making, and worth knowing you have made.

quote: Nobody is coming.
what_it_means: Three words did more work in this county than any three I know. Everything about a person in a disaster is built around waiting. You ration for a fortnight. You signal. You stay where the rescuers will look. You keep the road clear. All of that assumes an outside that is functioning, and there was not one. Accepting that is the moment a victim becomes a resident. The people who took it in during the first week planted in the first spring. The people who did not were still sitting in the loft in June with a torch and a whistle.
how_to_use_it: Somebody came. Twice, that I can document, both in the first month, both by boat. And the sentence turned into a licence, because it never once told anybody what to do next. It was used to justify not answering a knock, not walking to the next village, not looking for a woman's children. It is one of the four in this book that arrived already famous. No notebook and no body behind it. Worn smooth by three hundred retellings. There is a note at the back about how much that smoothness ought to worry you. It is the best sentence in the manual. That is what is wrong with it.

quote: Some people are staying. Let them, and stay with them if that is yours to do.
what_it_means: Not everybody can be moved. There is a ward of that in every town and there was one on Beckett Street. Nine people who could not walk. Two on oxygen. One who was four days from the end of a long illness that had nothing to do with any of this. Every rule in this chapter says leave. Trent's answer is that the arithmetic is correct about survival and has no jurisdiction over anything else. She stayed. She kept nine people comfortable for eleven days. In the circumstances of that fortnight that is a piece of work I cannot get to the bottom of. She wrote this on the ninth day, in a drug chart.
how_to_use_it: It is a rule that can be used on you. Up and down the county in that first fortnight, people were told they were staying, in a kind voice, by people who were leaving. The sentence in this entry is exactly the sentence they were told. Two of Trent's own nurses stayed because she had. They were twenty-four and twenty-six and they could have walked out on the first morning. A choice that is noble in the first person is coercion in the second, every time, with no exceptions I have found. So read it in the first person or do not read it at all. Nobody gets to make this one for anybody else. If you are reading it because somebody handed you the book open at this page, go.

quote: Write the date before you write anything else.
what_it_means: Time stops behaving. Without a written date the weeks fold up, and the folding costs you three things that matter. You lose the count on a bite, which is the difference between watching somebody and burying them. You lose the season, and this is a book about seasons. And you lose the ability to put two accounts side by side and see which came first. Okafor started the Long Room ledger on the fifth day with the date and the weather and nothing else, because that is what a librarian does when the world ends. Everything in this book has a day count on it because of her.
how_to_use_it: She kept the record and did not keep herself. There is no rule in her hand about food and she was seven stone in the second November. Beyond that, dates become a fetish. A group at Otley ran a calendar that had drifted nine days by the second spring. They planted on a written date instead of on a hedge coming into leaf, and lost most of a crop to a frost that the ledger said was over. The date is a tool for comparing accounts. The hedge is the authority on the hedge.

quote: A rumour that tells you where to go is a rumour somebody wants you to be.
what_it_means: Ask what a piece of information does when it enters a hundred heads. Most true things do nothing much. But a rumour that moves people moves them all in one direction, at one time, along one road, carrying everything they own, and there has never been a shortage of men who find that arrangement convenient. Pyle knew because he had spent his working life in the trade. Three of the four big movements in this county in the first year had somebody standing at the far end of them. The Kendal camp is the one everybody knows. There was no camp. There had never been a camp.
how_to_use_it: He was right and he used it. Two of the four movements were started by Pyle. Then there is the cost to everyone who believed the rule too well. A family on Dewsbury Road turned down three true offers of shelter in one winter, because each of them told them where to go. Two of the four died a hundred yards from a house with a fire in it. Suspicion of good news is expensive and it is not free of charge just because it is clever. Ask who benefits, then go and look at the place from a distance, then decide. Do not stop at the first step and call it wisdom.

quote: Believe the weather. Nothing else.
what_it_means: It is a rule about verifiability, and it has the merit of being usable by somebody with no training and no time. You can check a forecast by walking outside. You cannot check a report about Harrogate without going to Harrogate. Kite ran a set on car batteries from a bungalow at Guiseley and listened to everything that came over for eleven months. This is what he had to show for it. The weather was right about four times in five. Nothing else on the air was better than a coin.
how_to_use_it: There was one broadcast in the first year that was worth acting on, and it was not the weather. On the ninth of April a woman read out, four times, that the Aire valley was going to be opened up by a dam release, and Kite did not act, because it was not the weather. He lost his set and his bungalow and one of his two neighbours. A rule for filtering noise will filter the signal too, and it will do it on the one day of the year when that matters. Keep the rule and add a second sentence: anything that repeats itself four times gets a look out of the window.

quote: Nothing you hear about them is true unless you can name the person who watched it happen.
what_it_means: Look at what this rule killed. That it travels on the air. That fire frightens them, which cost a barn and nine people at Collingham. That running water stops them, which is a folk belief about something else entirely and which put two men in the Wharfe in February. That a fever means you are turning, which meant that in the first winter people were being put out of doors for having flu. Not one of those had a witness attached to it. Every one had a confident man attached to it. Errai's rule is the cheapest test there is, and it takes one question, and the question is who saw that.
how_to_use_it: The best thing anybody discovered has no author. Nobody knows who first worked out that they leave you alone if you smell enough like them. There is no witness, no notebook, no name. It works. It has saved more people than any other single fact in this manual. Errai's rule would have thrown it away. The rule is right about claims and wrong about techniques, and the difference is that a technique can be tested behind a wall by one person in an afternoon. Test what you can test. Doubt what you cannot.

quote: Two sources or it does not go on the board.
what_it_means: He ran a board in the Wetherby depot with three columns: heard, confirmed, acted on. Nothing crossed from the first column to the second without a second mouth that had not spoken to the first. It is the discipline of an operations room and it is the reason his group never once walked into an empty camp, in a year when four hundred people did. When a group is deciding whether to move eleven miles on a stranger's word, a board on a wall is worth more than any amount of good judgement in one man's head.
how_to_use_it: Two people repeating one rumour is one source wearing a coat, and telling the difference takes exactly the skill the board was built to replace. Worse is what it does to speed. On day 202 a boy came in and said the Aire had come over at Kirkstall, and there was nobody to confirm him. It sat in the first column for two days. By then eleven people were in the water. Hatherleigh added a line to the board that night, in different ink, and it is still there: a warning goes up on one source and comes down on two.

quote: Ask them what they were doing when they saw it.
what_it_means: It is the oldest question in the trade and it works because of how memory is built. A person who saw a thing was in the middle of something else at the time: carrying a box, arguing, looking for a dog. That detail comes back with the event attached to it and it comes back cheap and specific. A person who is repeating a story has no such detail, because there was no such afternoon. Okon separated true accounts from passed ones at the Hunslet gate for eight months, and it took him one question and about ten seconds.
how_to_use_it: Anybody good enough to be worth catching has thought about this. Pyle's accounts are full of the dog and the box, and they are full of them because he understood what the question is for. And the test punishes a particular kind of honest person: the shocked one, who has no detail at all, and whose account is flat and thin because it happened three hours ago to them and they have not slept. Twice in this book somebody was turned away at a gate for telling the truth badly. Use the question to find people to trust. Do not use it to find people to refuse.

quote: The map is four years old. So are you.
what_it_means: Reith is the only person in this book who has spent more of his life in this than before it, and it makes him worth listening to on a subject none of the rest of us are honest about. A map is a claim about a place, made at a date, by somebody who is not there now. The Kirkstall terraces are a field. Two viaducts are down. There is a lake where the retail park was, and it is on no map and it is nine feet deep. He walks with a map and treats it as a rumour with contours.
how_to_use_it: He went the other way with it and stopped believing written things at all, which is a young man's error and an expensive one. In the third summer he walked into the works at Knostrop, which is marked, clearly, on the four year old map, as a sewage treatment plant. He came out with something in a cut on his shin that nearly took the leg, and he was carried nine miles by two people who could ill afford the day. A map is out of date about buildings. It is not out of date about the ground, or the water, or where the poison was.

quote: Say that you do not know.
what_it_means: She came out of a trade where the words are said out loud and where saying them is a mark of competence, and she brought the habit with her into a world running on men who were certain. Here is the mechanism. A group can absorb the news that its leader does not know something. What it cannot absorb is discovering, later, that the leader did not know and said otherwise, because after that nothing that person says can be spent. Uncertainty said out loud is cheap. Uncertainty found out is the end of your authority in one afternoon.
how_to_use_it: There is a moment when a group needs a decision more than it needs an accurate account of your confidence. She hit it at Wetherby in the second January, with fourteen people standing in sleet waiting to be told which way. She told them what she did not know, at length, and she was completely honest, and they stood in it for forty minutes and two of them lost fingers. Say you do not know, then say what you are going to do anyway. The second half is not optional and it is the half she left out.

quote: Anybody certain about the biology has never watched one turn.
what_it_means: In the first spring every third man was an expert. The confidence was inverse to the exposure, exactly and reliably, and it is the cleanest example of the effect I have ever seen. The people who had sat with somebody through the six days would not tell you the shape of it, and would say the thing about how it varies, and were hedging because the world was hedging. Rahman had counted out other people's medicines for nineteen years and had a professional's ear for a man who has read one thing.
how_to_use_it: It disarms the person who did the work. Errai had the transmission route correct on day three, from evidence, and was dismissed for months by people quoting Rahman's rule at him, because he was certain and certainty was the tell. She has said since that it is the thing she regrets. Doubt a man's certainty, then ask him what it is built on, and if the answer is a pattern he counted himself then he is not the problem. The rule catches the confident. It does not distinguish between the confident and the correct, and you have to do that part yourself.

quote: Keep a book of what you were wrong about.
what_it_means: Three men with a generator broadcast the Kendal camp for eleven days and about four hundred people walked north on it. What they did afterwards is the reason they are in this manual. They kept a second book, read out every Sunday, of everything they had said that had turned out to be false. By the second year they were the only voice on the air that anybody in three counties trusted. You cannot get better at judging a claim without a record of your own misses, because memory quietly deletes them. Write them down and the deleting stops.
how_to_use_it: A list of a man's errors, in his own hand, is a weapon lying in the open. Skipton's book was used in the second winter to break the youngest of the three operators in front of a room of forty people, by somebody who wanted his position, and it worked, and he left. If you keep the book, keep it for one person. A group's book of its own errors is a fine idea and I have never once seen it survive a disagreement about food.

quote: You are allowed to believe something because you need to.
what_it_means: Four years is a long time to run on evidence alone and I have not met anybody who managed it. Moray's position, and she is careful about it, is that a belief has two properties and they are separate: whether it is true, and what it does to the person holding it. The man on Tong Road who is sure his daughter reached Ireland gets up in the morning. The one who worked out the odds does not. She is not telling you the odds are wrong. She is telling you that you are a piece of equipment that has to keep working, and that the maintenance of it is a legitimate thing to spend belief on.
how_to_use_it: The moment a belief starts costing anybody anything, it has stopped being maintenance and become a plan. Eleven people walked to Holyhead in the second autumn on a belief of this kind and four came back. And the sentence is the exact sentence that a certain sort of man says at the beginning of the thing he builds around himself. There have been two of those in this county and one of them is still going. Moray's own guard against it is worth copying. She holds one belief this way, she knows which one it is, she can name it, and she has never once asked anybody else to hold it with her.

quote: You cannot outwalk them. You can only stop being worth following.
what_it_means: Tait did the sum on the second Sunday, on the back of a leaflet, and it is the sum at the top of this chapter. Once you accept it, everything about how you move changes and it changes for the better. You stop thinking in miles and start thinking in corners. You stop grinding out an extra four miles at dusk, which is exactly when the ground gets worse and your judgement goes. You spend that energy on breaking line of sight, once, properly, and then walking away quietly. The people still alive in this county move in short deliberate legs between places they cannot be seen from. Nobody is doing forced marches. The forced marches are all in the notebooks that stop.
how_to_use_it: It is a rule for one of them, or four. It is not a rule for a drift. A drift of two thousand does not lose you, because the ones at the back are following the ones at the front, and the front is a mile wide. There is no corner that takes you out of sight of all of it. Tait knew this and wrote it, and the sentence that got copied around three counties is the short one, without the qualifier. I have had it quoted at me by a man who was proposing to walk across the front of a drift on the strength of it. Against a crowd, distance is the only thing that works, and you had better start early and you had better have somewhere to be.

quote: Twelve miles a day with a load, and no arguing about it.
what_it_means: It is a real number and it comes from a century of people measuring what a column can do day after day without falling apart. Twelve miles with weight is sustainable. Fifteen is a good day. Twenty is a day you pay for over the following two, and armies worked this out long before any of us needed it. The value of writing it down is that it stops the argument at four in the afternoon, when somebody is feeling strong and wants to push to the next town. The person feeling strong is never the person who will fail. Hatherleigh's group made the same distance every day for five weeks and arrived able to work.
how_to_use_it: It is a soldier's number, taken from fit men of similar age carrying similar loads, and his group had a woman of sixty-three, a boy of nine and a man who had been a bank clerk. A column moves at the speed of the person who is struggling, and if the number on the wall says twelve then what happens is not that everybody does twelve. What happens is that the woman of sixty-three does twelve and is destroyed by it, in silence, for four days, because she can read the number too. Set the day's distance from the slowest pair of legs and set it out loud. Then write that number on the wall.

quote: Never the road. The thing beside the road.
what_it_means: A road is the best navigation there is and it costs you everything else, because it is a corridor. Every walker, every drift and every man with a rifle and an idea is using the same corridor for the same reason. What Doherty worked out in his first fortnight is that you can have the navigation without the corridor. Walk the hedge line, the ditch, the field margin, the strip of scrub inside the fence. You are forty yards off. You can see the road and it cannot see you. You keep the direction and you keep the cover, and if something comes down the tarmac you lie down in a ditch and it goes past. He crossed the county four times in the first year and was seen twice.
how_to_use_it: It is half the speed on a good day and a third of it on a wet one, and a hedge line in February is a serious piece of work. The margins are also where everything is: the wire, the old wells, the drainage cuts under the grass, the badger holes. Doherty went into a rabbit hole on the flat, in daylight, in the second spring, and put his ankle out nine miles from anybody. He says himself that a man on the road would have been at Tadcaster by four. The road when you are strong and the time is short and you can see a long way. The hedge the rest of the time.

quote: Follow the cut.
what_it_means: A canal is the best walking in England and it always was. It is flat, because it has to be. It is waymarked to the quarter mile. It goes between towns without going through them. There is water in it, there are bridges every half mile that let you swap sides, and there are gates and locks that make a natural place to stop and see what is behind you. Cattermole had worked the Leeds and Liverpool for thirty-one years and could walk it in the dark, and eleven people came down it with him in the second April and every one arrived.
how_to_use_it: A towpath is a bottle. On one side is a hedge or a wall and on the other is the cut, and if something comes at you from both ends of a straight you have two options and one of them is the water. Here is the part people learn once. They do not drown. They do not float, they do not panic and they do not need to breathe. What happens when one goes in the canal is that it walks along the bottom. It comes out on the far bank six or seven minutes later, and it comes out where you are. Two of Cattermole's eleven found this out in the same afternoon. The cut is the best road in the county and it is the worst place to be surprised.

quote: Boots off at every stop. Every stop.
what_it_means: Skin that is wet for long enough stops being skin. It goes white, it goes soft, it comes off in sheets with the sock, and then you are a person who cannot walk in a world where walking is the only thing there is. Raghunathan saw four of these in one week in the first April and wrote the rule that night. Off, out, wrung, feet dry in the air for ten minutes, dry pair on, wet pair inside the coat against the body where they will be half dry in two hours. Ten minutes an hour is expensive. A foot is more expensive, and unlike almost everything else in this book, a ruined foot cannot be traded for, prayed over or fixed later.
how_to_use_it: There is a stop where you cannot afford eight minutes and you will not know it is that stop until it is. A man called Devlin died at Micklefield in the second November sitting on a wall with both boots off and both socks in his hands, and he had done everything right for two hundred days. The rule needs its exception said out loud so that people can use it: boots off at every stop where somebody else is watching the ground. Alone, or with one other, you dry your feet at the place you are sleeping and nowhere else.

quote: Move at four in the morning.
what_it_means: Four in the morning is the coldest hour of the day, and cold is the one thing that reliably takes them apart. Below four degrees they are slow and stupid. In a hard frost they stop where they stand and become street furniture that you walk around. So the coldest hour is the hour when a thing that is faster than you is not faster than you. It is also the hour when every human being for nine miles is asleep, which in this county matters at least as much. Anand had been riding a bike round this city at that hour for six years before any of it and knew the streets in the dark better than in the light.
how_to_use_it: You cannot see, and everything in the last four entries about the ditch and the wire and the ankle is four times as likely in the dark. The cold that slows them slows you first and slows you more. You are the one who has been asleep and is now walking at two miles an hour with no breakfast. Hypothermia does not need a hard winter to work on a thin person at four in the morning. And in July four in the morning is fourteen degrees, and they are as quick then as at noon. This is a rule for October to March. In summer it is just walking in the dark for no advantage, and Anand herself stopped doing it in the second June.

quote: Carry the means to drink, not the drink.
what_it_means: Water is two and a bit pounds a litre and you need three or four litres a day, and if you carry that you are carrying eight or nine pounds of the twenty-five you can carry at all. But this is England. There is water every mile, in gutters, streams, tanks, roofs, radiators and the header tank of every loft you pass. What you lack is not water, it is water you dare drink. Prydderch carried a litre, a filter, a bottle of tablets and a small pan, which came to under three pounds, and she drank six litres a day for two years and was never once ill. The weight you save goes into food, which is the thing there is genuinely not enough of.
how_to_use_it: Means fail and water does not. A filter clogs, and it clogs without warning on the day you push it through silt. Tablets get wet. A pan needs fire and fire is chapter five's problem. In the second August there was a stretch across the flat land east of here with twenty miles and nothing in it, in a summer when everything standing had gone green and foul. The man carrying four litres of stupid heavy water walked it. The two people carrying filters did not. Carry the means. Then carry a litre anyway, and be aware of what it is for, which is the day the means let you down.

quote: Walk to somewhere. Never away from something.
what_it_means: Retreat has no end condition. That is the whole argument and it is a good one. A group that is moving away from a thing will keep moving, because there is no distance at which anybody can say we have arrived. So it walks until it is too tired to make decisions, and then it makes one. A named place fixes that. It fixes the day's distance. It fixes the direction when you are tired. It gives you something to talk about at night that is not what you left. And it lets the argument happen at the map, and not at four in the afternoon in the rain. It does not have to be a good place. It has to be a place with a name.
how_to_use_it: A named place is a thing you press on towards, and everybody who has climbed knows what that does, and Semenova knew it better than anybody in this book and did it anyway. Her group had Malham in their heads. They kept the number of days it would take and they kept it after the weather turned and after the older of the two brothers started coughing. Turning back means admitting the plan was the problem, and the plan was hers. They got to Malham. Two of the five got to Malham. A destination is a tool for making decisions and it becomes, without anybody noticing the hour it happens, a reason not to make them.

quote: Nothing in the bag that you have not carried up a hill.
what_it_means: Everything is light for the first mile. That is the trap. It is why every abandoned pack on every verge in this county has the same four things in it, and why the verges of the first spring were a museum of what people thought they needed on a Tuesday. Adjei loaded her bag on the second day, walked it up the hill at Beeston and back down, and took out a third of it. She did that three times over a fortnight, until what was left was what she could carry all day. Twenty-five pounds is a load. Thirty-five is a load you will put down in a hurry one day, and the day you put it down is the day you needed it.
how_to_use_it: Watch what people cut. They cut the thing they have not used yet. The things you have not used yet are the medical kit, the spare socks and the second knife, and those are the items whose entire purpose is the day that has not happened. Adjei cut her kit down to a beautiful weight over three weeks and had no dressings in it at all when a woman in her group opened her hand on a gate in June. Weigh the bag. Then take the medical kit out, put it on the floor, and pack it first, and let everything else compete for what is left.

quote: Run for the corner. Then walk.
what_it_means: It is the practical form of the sum at the top of this chapter. Running does not get you away, because nothing gets you away. Running gets you round the corner, over the wall, into the alley, out of sight, and then its whole job is done. Continuing to run is now working against you, because running is loud, and loud recruits. The thing you have just lost has friends within earshot who have not seen you at all yet. Sprint for as long as it takes to break the line. Then stop, breathe through your nose, and walk out of the area at a speed that makes no noise on gravel. Reith has done this several hundred times and he is twenty years old and he is very hard to kill.
how_to_use_it: The corner has to be a real corner. A corner that leads into a yard is not a corner. It is a room with a door in it. The whole method depends on knowing what is round the thing you are about to run round, which means it belongs to people who know the ground. Reith grew up on this ground. The woman he was with in the second winter did not, and she could not do the second half of it. She kept running because everything in her body was telling her to. The noise of it across two hundred yards of car park brought in what was in the multi storey. He got round the corner and walked. She did not. He has written about it once and I am not going to add anything to it.

quote: Stop walking.
what_it_means: The roaming years killed more people than they saved and the notebooks are not subtle about it. Walking is exposure, every day, all day, and it produces nothing: no store, no crop, no roof, no fence, no relationships with anybody who might help you in February. Lunt watched three groups pass her gate in the first year, all of them going somewhere better. She was still on her land when the third of them came back past, going the other way, with fewer people in it. Everybody alive round here at scale is somebody who stopped. The rule gives you permission to be the person who is not moving, in a year when moving looked like the only competence there was.
how_to_use_it: She stopped on eleven acres with a spring on it, a stone barn, walls she could see over and a slope that meant nothing could come at her out of dead ground. That is not stopping. That is stopping somewhere, and the somewhere is doing all the work in the sentence. Two settlements I could name stopped in the wrong place and stayed out of the same instinct. They defended it past the point where anybody with clear eyes would have walked out, and were finished in the second summer inside a week. Stopping is right. Being unable to leave the place you stopped is the same disease as never stopping at all, and it is chapter four's subject, and Lunt keeps a bag packed by her door to this day.

quote: Count the doors before you count the exits.
what_it_means: Bello's point is that people survey a building for how things get in, which is a list of doors, and then believe they have surveyed it. The useful list is a different list with different members. An exit is a door you can go through, in the dark, in a hurry, carrying somebody, with whatever tool is in your pocket. A door you have screwed, barred, filled or bricked is not on that list any more. He walked buildings with two counts in two columns and made people say both numbers out loud. In a leisure centre, a chapel and two schools those numbers came out very far apart.
how_to_use_it: He counted eleven doors in the leisure centre at Cottingley and made all eleven fast. When the fire took the east stand there were eleven doors and no exits, because he had welded the difference out of the building. That is the whole of it, and he was the best man at that trade in this half of the city, and he had been reasoning correctly the entire way. What he lacked was a rule about which of the two numbers is allowed to reach zero. Make the doors hard. Leave two of them, on different walls, that a frightened person can open with their hands, and tell everybody in the building which two they are.

quote: Wedge. Do not lock.
what_it_means: A wedge under a door that opens towards you is close to unbeatable by anything without a shoulder and a plan, and it has four properties a lock does not. It is silent going in. It needs no key, so nobody is ever the wrong side of it. It works on any door in any building you walk into, including the one you have been in for eleven minutes. And it comes out with a kick when you have decided to go, which no bar, screw or barricade does. Okon carried six of them cut from a fence post and got through the whole of the second year on nothing else.
how_to_use_it: Wedges want a floor. On carpet they ride. On a worn stone flag they skate. On a door with a quarter inch under it they do nothing at all, and you find this out at two in the morning. They are also a fine defence against a push and a poor one against a sustained lean. That is what a crowd is. A crowd does not push. It arrives and continues to be there. Okon's own note is that a wedge buys you between forty seconds and four minutes, and that the number is not the point. The point is that the forty seconds are yours to use, and if you have not decided in advance what you are going to do with them then you have bought nothing.

quote: Glass is not a wall. Glass is a curtain.
what_it_means: Go and look at a house that was lost in the first year and the door is nearly always intact. People fortify what they think of as the way in. The way in was the bay window in the front room, four feet of nine hundred millimetre float glass that a wheelie bin goes through by falling on it. Prentice had spent twenty years working outside buildings and had a glazier's view of what a house actually is, which is a light frame with big holes in it and some plaster. His rule reorders the work: the ground floor openings first, all of them, before anybody touches a door.
how_to_use_it: He boarded a whole ground floor in Armley in three days and then had to live in it. A house with every opening blinded is a house where nobody can see out. Not being able to see out is worse than most of what you were afraid of seeing. Every decision about going outside is now made blind. The people in that house began to go out to find out what was happening, which is the exact behaviour the boards were meant to prevent. Board the glass. Then cut a slot at eye height in two boards on two different walls, and accept the small risk that comes with them. The alternative is a group that has to open the front door to learn anything.

quote: Sleep where you have to be lifted to.
what_it_means: They do not climb. They manage stairs, badly, because stairs are a floor at an angle and their legs still work. A ladder is not a floor at an angle. Anything that needs a hand on a rung and a decision about where the next foot goes is outside what they can do. It always has been. It is the most reliable single fact about them after the cold. So: a hayloft with the ladder pulled up. A flat roof reached by a scaffold plank you draw in. A first floor with the stairs taken out and a rope ladder in the hole. Any of those turns eight hours of unconsciousness from the most dangerous part of your day into the safest.
how_to_use_it: People. A rope ladder is a wonderful defence against a thing that cannot think, and a signpost to a thing that can. Semenova was robbed twice in a loft she could not get out of, by men who stood at the bottom and waited. It took them no effort at all. There is also the ordinary failure. She broke a wrist coming down in the dark at speed in the second November, in a hurry, for a reason that turned out to be a fox. Every night for a year she had climbed up and been safe. It took one descent to cost her four months of work.

quote: Two ways out of any room you sleep in.
what_it_means: She ran fire drills for twenty-two years and she brought the finding with her. What people do in the first eleven seconds of being woken by an emergency is go back the way they came in, all of them, together. If that way is blocked they stop and stand in it. A second exit does not merely double your chances. It halves the crowd at the first one, which is the thing that kills. Kaminski made every group she was ever part of walk both exits, in the dark, twice, on the night they arrived, and no group of hers has ever lost anybody in a building.
how_to_use_it: Two ways out is two ways in, and the whole of chapter four is an argument about that trade. Her old school had fourteen exits and was the most indefensible building in the district, and she is clear that she would not sleep in it. There is a second failure that is subtler. A group that has drilled its exits will use them. Using an exit means going outside at night with no information. Twice in these notebooks a group has gone out of the back door into something worse, because a bin fell over at the front. The drill is right. Add one word to it: everybody goes to the second exit, and nobody goes through it until somebody has looked.

quote: The smallest room you can stand.
what_it_means: This is the entry that has saved the most lives in this chapter and it will not feel like it in November. A body puts out about the heat of a bulb. Three bodies and one candle will hold a box room above freezing all night with the door shut. Nothing you own will do that for a Victorian front room with a nine foot ceiling and a chimney in it. In the first February people froze in beautiful houses with fuel still in the yard. They were heating a volume instead of a space. Quaye moved five people into a back scullery eight feet by seven and hung blankets over the door and the window. They came through the worst month any of us have seen without a single case of anything.
how_to_use_it: Five people in a room eight feet by seven, in the dark, for four months, is a thing that happens to your mind. Two of his five stopped speaking to each other in that scullery over something neither of them can now reconstruct, and one of them left in the spring and did not come back. Small rooms preserve the body and grind the group, and the grinding does not show up until March, and by March it is done. Take the room. Then build the day around getting people out of it in ones and twos for an hour, in daylight, doing something with their hands, whatever the weather is doing. Treat that hour as fuel and not as leisure.

quote: Bells.
what_it_means: You cannot watch. That is the fact underneath every perimeter anybody has ever built. A group of six cannot keep a pair of eyes awake and useful on three approaches for six months. The ones that tried burned out in a fortnight and then slept through everything. So the ground watches instead. Bramall ran fine wire at shin height through the hedges at thirty yards out, with tins and two brass bells off a harness. He could sleep. He had not slept properly since March. The distance matters more than the noise: thirty yards is far enough that the sound reaches you before the thing does and near enough that you know it is your problem.
how_to_use_it: Alarm fatigue, and it is merciless. Foxes, cats, wind, a badger every night for a week. By the fortieth false alarm nobody is getting up, and the wire is now a thing that ruins everybody's sleep without protecting anything. Bramall's group had stopped rising to it well before the night that mattered. The fix he arrived at in the second year is the one worth copying: two lines, at different distances, with different sounds. The far one is information and you note it and stay in bed. The near one has never once been an animal, and when it goes everybody moves.

quote: Leave the bodies in the street.
what_it_means: It is the most unpleasant rule in this book and it is sound. A street with bodies in it reads, at a hundred yards, as a street that has already been done. The thing you most want in the second year is to be uninteresting to people. It does more than that. The smell covers yours, which matters, because smell is how they sort each other out. Doherty lived a whole winter on a terrace that four separate groups walked past, and one of them stopped at the end of it, and looked, and went the other way.
how_to_use_it: Rats came, and then everything rats bring, and by the second August the flies were a serious medical problem and two of his household had something they could not shake. There is also what it does to people to live in it, which he does not write about and which the people who were there do. And once, on his own doorstep in the second March, one of them was not a body. It had been lying in the same position for eleven days in the cold, doing nothing, because in the cold that is what they do, and it stood up when the thaw came. Cold ones are not dead ones. If you are going to use this rule, you put a spike through every head on your street. You do it in the frost, when it is safe to. And you write down how many there are.

quote: The smoke, not the flame.
what_it_means: Everybody worries about the fire being seen and hardly anybody does the arithmetic on the smoke. At night a flame in a window is visible for two or three miles and you can cover a window. By day a column of smoke off a wet fire is visible for eight or nine, and you can cover nothing. In the first winter you could stand on the ridge above here at ten in the morning. And count the households. Ferrier's method is the one the estates used for a century. Burn dry hardwood. Burn it hot and small. Burn in the middle of the day, when the sky is already grey and the air is turbulent. Put it under a long cold flue that breaks the column up.
how_to_use_it: It gives you one hot meal a day, at a time chosen by the weather. It is very hard to run a household of children on a fire that is only lit under cloud. The second failure is the one that got him. His flue trick works because moving air pulls the plume apart. On the still bright morning of the fourth of December there was no moving air at all. The smoke went up out of that chimney in a rope you could see from Otley. He had used the same fire for a hundred days. Weather is not a background condition. It is a member of the household, and it gets a vote every morning.

quote: The best wall is a bad approach.
what_it_means: You cannot build a wall. Be honest about the labour. A family, in a fortnight, with hand tools, cannot build anything that will hold against a serious push. Every hour spent on it is an hour not spent on the store and the crop. What you can do is choose ground where the approach does the work for free. A single track with a drop on one side. A spur with water on two. A slope steep enough that anything coming up it is slow and in the open and visible for four minutes. Lunt's place has one way in, uphill, in view of the house for three hundred yards, and she has never had to defend it because nothing has ever got near it unseen.
how_to_use_it: A bad approach is bad in both directions. Everything she owns has come up that track on her back or on a pony. In the second winter the snow filled the cut, and nothing came up or down it for five weeks. There was a woman in that house who needed a doctor. And good ground is legible to anybody who reads ground. Twice in these notebooks a settlement has been found by people with rifles, because the terrain around it was the terrain anybody would choose. That is a strange and specific way to be caught. It has happened more than once.

quote: It is a house. Leave it.
what_it_means: She spent thirty days making a house in Norfolk safe, and it was good work. On the thirty-first she put four things in a bag, walked out of it and never went back. The water had gone bad and she could count. That is the whole content of the rule and it is the hardest sentence in this chapter to actually perform. A shelter you have worked on becomes a thing you are unwilling to lose, and the unwillingness arrives quietly and dressed as sense. By the time it is obvious, you are a person arguing that the water is probably fine. Everything you built was to keep you alive. When it stops doing that, it is timber.
how_to_use_it: Leaving is a real cost and not a free move. There is a kind of person who reads this rule and becomes unable to commit to anything, and drifts for three years accumulating nothing, and is thin. Winslow left one house in four years and settled the second time. The rule is not walk away easily. It is that the walking away must remain possible. The bag stays packed. The two exits stay clear. And the decision gets made on the evidence rather than on the labour already spent. She keeps the key to the Norfolk house on a string. She has never suggested going back for it.

quote: Low and long carries. Sharp and short does not.
attribution: Femi Adeyemi, live sound engineer, day 35
what_it_means: He had spent eleven years putting sound into rooms and knew, without having to reason about it, which parts of a noise survive a journey. Air absorbs the top end. Foliage absorbs the top end. A brick wall stops the top end and lets the bottom walk round the corner. So the practical ranking is not by how loud a thing is in your hand. It is a generator, a diesel engine, a pump, a big steady voice, a hammer on wood, an axe. And then a very long way down, everything sharp and small that people are afraid of. Adeyemi ranked the household's noises on a sheet of paper in the second month, and the sheet is still pinned up in three settlements I know of.
how_to_use_it: Distance is one axis and novelty is the other, and he built his method on the first and forgot the second. What turns a head near you is not the loudest thing, it is the thing that was not there a second ago. A steady hum becomes background inside a minute, to them as much as to you, and a single tap in a silent street at four in the morning is the most attention-getting sound a human being can make. He was killed by neither, as it happens. He was killed on the ridge above Bramley by a piece of corrugated sheet that he stood on, which is short, sharp, and was the only sound in a quarter of a mile.

quote: Shoes at the door, felt on everything, cloth in the cutlery drawer.
what_it_means: A house makes a sound whether anybody is being careful or not, and it is made of about thirty things: two hinges, a latch, four floorboards, a stair tread, a bucket handle, a kettle lid, the drawer. Winslow's method was to find all thirty in one afternoon and fix them, because a fault you have fixed costs nothing thereafter and a fault you are being careful about costs attention every hour of every day for four years. Grease on the hinges, felt under the bucket, a strip of blanket over the drawer runners, and a nail through the loose tread. After that the household can move normally, which is the entire point and the part people miss.
how_to_use_it: A silent house is a house you cannot hear anybody moving in, including somebody who is not supposed to be there. Winslow's second household had a man walk the length of the ground floor and out again with most of a week's food. Four people were awake upstairs. She now leaves one board loose on purpose, at the bottom of the stairs, and everybody knows which. The other cost is speed. People who have been trained out of noise move slowly at exactly the moments when they should be moving fast. There is at least one death in these notebooks that comes down to a woman closing a door quietly instead of running through it.

quote: Loud work in the rain.
what_it_means: Rain on leaves and roofs is broadband noise across the whole range, which is the only thing that masks properly, and hard rain will take twenty feet of chopping and reduce it to something you cannot pick out at a hundred. Wind in trees does the same job less reliably. A river does it all the time in one place, which is why the mills were always the noisiest buildings in England. Mackay ran a rule that any job involving an axe, a hammer, a saw or a scream waited for weather, and she got her boat repaired, her shed built and two winters of firewood done in the rain.
how_to_use_it: Masking works both ways and there is no version where it does not. You cannot hear them either, and you cannot hear a person, and hard rain takes your eyes down to about sixty yards as well. She lost a man off the staithe at Paull in the second October to something that walked up behind him in weather that was doing exactly what she had planned for it to do. Rain is also when everything is slippery and cold and your hands are bad. Do the loud work in the rain. Put somebody on the corner who is doing nothing but looking, and rotate them, because looking at nothing in the rain for an hour is harder than the work.

quote: Two taps come here. Three taps run. There is nothing else.
what_it_means: Whatever signalling system you design, the version that gets used is the version people can perform while frightened, and that is a very short list. Two signals is a list people can perform. Kaminski had watched twenty-two years of children under drill conditions and she knew that the vocabulary shrinks to nothing under stress, so she built for the worst state rather than the calm one. Tapping also has the right acoustics, which she did not know and got right by accident: a knuckle on wood is mid-range and directional and it does not carry past the building.
how_to_use_it: A vocabulary of two cannot say the thing that most needs saying. There is no signal in that system for I am hurt and I am not in danger. On the eleventh of March in the second year a boy called Aaron Petch tapped three, which means run, because it was the only thing he had. The household ran. He had a broken leg under a fallen gate two hundred yards away, and they were a mile off before anybody worked it out. He was alive when they came back the next morning and he was not there. Add a third signal. Add only one, and make it mean come slowly and bring the bag.

quote: Never shout a name.
what_it_means: A human voice calling a name is the most effective recruiting sound there is and it beats a gunshot, which surprises people. A shot is one event, over in a fifth of a second, and half a mile away it is a thing that might have been a door. A name is a voice, pitched where voices are pitched, repeated, getting louder each time because you are getting more frightened, going on for a minute or more. It says a person is here, it says where, and it says that person is distressed and stationary. Raghunathan had watched it happen twice in a hospital car park and never shouted again.
how_to_use_it: A rule against calling out is a rule against calling for help, and it does not distinguish. Her own group carried it too far and got quiet about everything. A woman named Ruth Colley went into a flooded cellar on Barkerend Road after a dropped box and was in there for two days. There were four people in the house above her. They had all heard something, and had all decided on their own not to shout. Nobody in these notebooks ever mentions this. It is the failure of the good pupils. Take the rule as written for open ground, and hang the opposite of it on the inside of the door: in this building we call out, and we call out early, and we do not wait to be sure.

quote: The generator runs one hour a week.
what_it_means: A small petrol set is around sixty-five decibels of low-frequency noise at a couple of yards, which is not much, and it is unbroken, and unbroken is what does the damage. Everything within a mile that can hear it has all afternoon to walk towards it, and unlike a bang, it does not stop and let them lose interest. Kite worked out in the first autumn that his set was not attracting things from a distance, it was accumulating them over days, and the crowd at the bottom of the lane was the sum of a fortnight of Wednesdays. One hour a week, in daylight, in wind, with the set in a pit under a straw bale.
how_to_use_it: Rationing the power rationed the listening, and the listening was the entire point of the machine. He was off the air for the six days that mattered most in the second year and heard the news about the Bradford road eleven days after everybody else. The bigger failure was the schedule. One hour a week is one hour a week at the same time, because that is what a schedule is. By the third summer there was a man who knew when Kite's set ran, and he had told other people. They came on a Wednesday. A ration is right. Roll the day and the hour every week, and take the small cost of being unpredictable to your friends as well.

quote: If you want a street quiet, make a noise in the next one.
what_it_means: They follow sound and they keep following it while it lasts, and they do not check whether the sound is a person. A wind-up alarm clock in the footwell of a car with the window down will run for twenty minutes and hold a drift's attention for an afternoon. Once the front of a crowd is moving, the back of it follows the front. No clock is needed after that. It is the cheapest tactic in this book. Pyle used it to empty the whole of a shopping parade at Hunslet, twice, and walked in behind them with a wheelbarrow, and there is no arguing with the results.
how_to_use_it: You have not removed a crowd. You have aimed it. Whatever comes to the clock is now two streets from where it was, in a place you chose and did not look at first. On the second occasion the parade Pyle emptied was three hundred yards from the almshouses on Church Street. There were eleven people in there who had been getting away with it since the first spring. Six of them. He is the only person in this book who has written down a thing of that kind about himself, which is a point in his favour and is not very many points. Look at where the noise is going. It is going to somebody.

quote: Muffle the dog. Do not get rid of the dog.
what_it_means: A dog is the best perimeter anybody has and nothing built out of wire and tins comes close. It smells them at two hundred yards, upwind and in the dark, and it knows the difference between a fox and a man, which no bell has ever managed. The problem is only the barking, and barking is trainable, and Ferrier had trained working dogs for twenty years. What he taught was a silent alert: the dog comes to you, presses its head against your leg, and holds. Two of the settlements up the valley run his dogs' grandchildren and neither has been surprised in two years.
how_to_use_it: That training takes a calm handler, a hundred repetitions and about four months, and almost nobody in the first year had any of the three. What most people had was an ordinary frightened family dog, which barks, and a rule from a gamekeeper saying keep the dog. There are at least four households in these notebooks that were found because of a dog they had been told not to get rid of. A dog costs about the food of a small adult, every day, all year. Keep the dog if you can train it or it is already trained. Otherwise you are keeping an alarm that goes off at the wrong things and eats.

quote: Nothing is answered after dark.
what_it_means: At night the air above the ground is warmer than the ground, and that bends sound downward and keeps it travelling, so a voice at two in the morning reaches two or three times as far as the same voice at noon. That is the physics, and the human consequence is that anybody calling in the dark has chosen the ground, knows you cannot see, and has the whole night to work with. Doherty's household answered nothing between dusk and light for three years, on any pretext, and were never once robbed, and he is a man who had a great deal worth taking.
how_to_use_it: Real people call at night, because night is when things go wrong. A boy walked up the Elland Road side of the estate in the second February calling for anybody, for about forty minutes, in a hard frost. Eleven households heard him and every single one of them had this rule. He was found in the morning between two cars. There is no version of this where everybody follows the rule and that boy lives. The revision people have arrived at up here has three parts. You do not answer with your voice. You do not open your door. You put a light in a window that means come to the light at dawn, and somebody watches the light all night. It is not much. It would have been enough for him.

quote: Silence is a season. It is not a rule.
attribution: Femi Adeyemi, live sound engineer, day 300
what_it_means: This is the correction to his own first entry and to most of this chapter. A household needs to chop, build, hammer, dig, argue and sing. If all of that is forbidden then none of it happens. A group that does none of it for a year has no fuel, no repairs and no way of being a group. So you budget noise instead of banning it, and you spend the budget when it is cheapest, and in this country that means the frost. Below freezing they are standing still. Wind and rain mask. Winter is when you take the roof off and put a new one on, and there is a rhythm to the year up here now that comes directly out of this sentence.
how_to_use_it: A budget with permission in it gets spent, and then gets spent again, and the drift is invisible from inside. Adeyemi's own settlement went from an axe in a January frost to a forge running in October in about eighteen months, one reasonable decision at a time, with nobody at any point doing anything indefensible. That is how it always goes. Somebody has to hold the number, out loud, and be unpopular. Adeyemi's note is that the person holding it should not be the person who decides what the work is. Those two jobs in one head is how the number moves.

quote: Make some noise.
what_it_means: Quaye cut hair on Peckham High Street for nineteen years and his position is that a settlement of people who have whispered for four years is not a settlement, it is forty individuals standing near each other. Sound is most of how people are together. Singing, arguing across a yard, a child shouting, the noise of a room where something is being made. He started a Sunday in the frost where the rule is suspended for three hours between the wall and the barn: instruments, talking at a normal volume, and a haircut. Attendance is total. Two of the four settlements up this valley have copied it and both of them report the same thing, which is that people stopped leaving.
how_to_use_it: It was quiet for a reason and the reason has not gone anywhere. A settlement at Guiseley took up a version of this in the second year, without the frost condition and without the walls. They were found in the autumn by people, not by them. There are nine of them left out of thirty-one. Quaye's rule has three conditions on it and they are all load-bearing: hard ground, hard frost, and a wall you have walked yourself that week. He has never once suspended it for a wedding in June, and he has been asked, and the asking is the hardest part of the job.

quote: Boil it. If you did not watch it boil, boil it.
what_it_means: A minute at a rolling boil finishes everything biological that this country has to offer, and biological is what kills you. All the dysentery in these notebooks. The thing that went through the Kirkstall camp in the second July and took nineteen people in nine days. Prydderch's second sentence is the one that matters. Water that somebody says is boiled is not boiled. The failures are all social rather than technical. The person who let it off at a simmer was tired and it was late and it looked like it was going. She ran one pot, one fire, one named person a day, and that household has not had a case in three years.
how_to_use_it: Boiling is expensive and it fixes only one of the two problems. It costs wood, which costs cutting, which is noise and exposure, and a household of six needs eighteen litres a day and that is a real fire every day forever. It does nothing to what came out of the works at Knostrop, or off the fields, or out of a tank with a dead pigeon and four years of lead in it. And boiled water in a warm store is fine for two days and is not sterile after that. It goes back to being ordinary water the moment it is standing in a bucket in a kitchen. Boil it, cover it, and use it inside two days.

quote: The latrine goes downhill of the water and further away than you want it.
what_it_means: Thirty yards and downhill of anything you drink, and that number is not a superstition, it is roughly how far it takes ordinary ground to do the filtering. Everything Prydderch's entry is about gets into the water at this one point. The camps that failed in the first two years failed here more than anywhere else. They failed within about six weeks of setting up, every time, in the same way. Okonjo had delivered babies in places with no plumbing. She knew that the whole of public health, when you take the pipes away, is one hole in the right place and a rule about hands.
how_to_use_it: A latrine thirty yards away is not used at three in the morning in February by a woman with dysentery. That is not a failure of character. It is arithmetic about a person who is ill in the dark and cold. What happens instead is behind the shed, ten feet from the door, which is worse than having no rule at all because nobody is admitting to it. Okonjo's own correction took her a year to write down. The rule has two halves and everybody publishes the first. The hole goes thirty yards downhill, and a covered bucket goes by the door. The bucket is emptied into the hole by whoever is up first, and nobody is ever asked about it.

quote: Perishables first. The tins are for February.
what_it_means: It is the order every quartermaster has used and it is right for the reason that is easy to miss. You are not choosing what to eat. You are choosing what to throw away. Anything with a short life is either eaten now or lost entirely, and a tin loses nothing by waiting a year. So the fresh goes first, then the dry, then the tinned, and the shape of the store you end up with in January is the shape you would have designed. Hatherleigh's depot came out of the first winter with four months in hand when three groups within five miles were eating candles.
how_to_use_it: It assumes there is a February and that you are in it. Two households in these papers ate to a plan for a spring they did not reach, and left stores behind them that other people are eating now. That is not the worst outcome in the book. It is not what they were planning. The subtler failure is what it does to the autumn. Heavy work happens in September and October. The plan has you eating the thin end of the perishables then, and the good tinned fat in February when you are sitting still. That is backwards for the body doing the work. Feed the season you are in. Move about a fortnight of the good food forwards into the digging.

quote: Salt, fat, and something green.
what_it_means: These are the three things a scavenged diet lacks and each one kills differently. Without fat you can eat rabbit until your jaw aches and starve doing it, which happened to at least two people in these notebooks and which reads like nonsense until you understand it. Without salt you cannot work in July and cannot keep anything through October. Without something green you have about three months before your gums go and your old wounds open. There were people in the second March who thought they had been bitten and had scurvy. Lawal knew every one of these from the trade and he wrote the rule so that a person who could not cook could still eat correctly.
how_to_use_it: Something green in February costs more than it returns. Going out for four hours in the cold for a handful of nettles that are not there yet is a bad trade in calories and a worse one in exposure. The answer is not the winter forage. It is the autumn one, dried and hung. His own household's failure was different and it is a professional's failure. He had them cooking, beautifully, every day, and not preserving. They came out of the second autumn with the best food anybody had eaten in a year, and eleven weeks of store where they should have had twenty.

quote: Plant more than you can eat and less than you can weed.
what_it_means: Everybody who has never grown anything believes the constraint is seed and it is not, it is labour in June. A plot that is twice what you can keep on top of does not give you twice the food. It gives you a field of weeds with some potatoes in it, and it takes the same ground and the same water. Lunt's rule sets the size by the bottleneck rather than by the ambition. The households up this valley that took it seriously are the ones with a store. The ones that dug up half a hillside in the first optimistic April fed the rabbits.
how_to_use_it: A crop is a fixed asset and a beacon. It is visible from a distance, it cannot be moved, it announces the number of people it is meant to feed, and it ripens on a date that anybody watching can also read. Two settlements in these notebooks were robbed at exactly the right week by people who had done nothing all year but wait. Then there is the ordinary agricultural disaster. She went into the second year on potatoes, because potatoes are the calories, and the blight came through in August. She has planted four things every year since and expects to lose one of them.

quote: Learn one animal properly.
what_it_means: A person who half knows chickens, rabbits, goats and bees has four things that will die on him and no idea which. A person who knows one, in detail, through a full year, has a thing that produces food without being hunted for. It turns grass or scraps or flowers into calories while he is asleep. Bramall had kept bees for thirty years and got honey, wax for light, and a swarm to trade, out of hives he did not have to feed at all. The knowledge is the asset. Everybody can acquire the animal.
how_to_use_it: One animal is one bad winter away from nothing, and his was the second one. He lost every colony he had between December and February, to cold and to a mite he had no treatment for. A man who has spent two years being the person with the bees turns out to have no second thing. And no time to learn one at fifty-eight. He is alive because his neighbours fed him through a spring. Know one animal properly. Then spend one afternoon a month being an amateur at a second, and be content to be bad at it. Bad at two is the position Bramall would have wanted in that February.

quote: A tooth will kill you sooner than a bite.
what_it_means: Count them in the notebooks. After the cold and the water, the next thing on the list is jaws, and it is a long way ahead of anything with teeth of its own. An abscess in a lower molar has a short road into the floor of the mouth and the neck. From there it is days. There is no surgeon and no antibiotic worth the name in this county. The diet does not help: nothing sweet any more, which people think saves them, but everything is gritty and acid and hard, and enamel goes. Kowal's regime is a rag, salt and two minutes, every night, for everybody, forever, and she checks mouths on the first Sunday of the month like a schoolteacher.
how_to_use_it: She began pulling teeth in the second summer because there was nobody else, and she is a hairdresser, and she says so on the page in a way I have not softened. Eleven extractions. Three went badly, one of those very badly, and a woman who had a treatable abscess in March had a broken root and a worse infection in April. The rule also drives people towards the pliers too early, because a rule that says teeth kill makes every ache an emergency. Clean the mouth every day and you will not need the pliers. That is the entry. The pulling is not the technique, it is the confession of the technique having failed.

quote: Six days, in a room with a door that opens from the outside.
what_it_means: Turning takes between four hours and nine days and the spread is not random. It goes with body mass and with how much got in. A small child bitten badly is hours. A heavy man with a graze is most of a week. That is the whole of the science and it is enough to act on. Errai's protocol is the one that has held up. The bitten person goes in a room alone, with water, with light, with the door bolted on the outside and a hatch. Somebody sits with them and talks to them through it. Nobody is tied up. The last part is not sentiment. Restraint has killed people in these papers who were never infected at all, of thirst, of cold, and once of a fire.
how_to_use_it: Six is not nine. He chose six because six covers most cases and because a household cannot hold a room and a watcher for nine days. He has written, twice, that this was a compromise with the labour available and not a finding. Two people in these notebooks came out of that room on the sixth day and turned on the seventh, and one of those took three others with him. And the protocol is unbearable in a way that no writing conveys. It is a rule for a stranger. Almost nobody has ever managed to perform it on their own child, and I am not going to pretend the failure rate there is anything other than total.

quote: Cut it off.
what_it_means: It is in the book because it works sometimes and because a rumour that it never works has cost lives. There are eleven amputations in these notebooks, all of them below a knee or an elbow, all within a few minutes of the bite. Three of those people are alive and none of the three turned. The reasoning is that it does not travel instantly and a limb removed above the wound at speed can take the whole of it. That is the entire basis. It is thinner than anybody would like. Raghunathan wrote it out as a procedure, with a tourniquet, a time and an order of operations. If it is going to be done at all, it will be done by somebody who is not a nurse.
how_to_use_it: Eight of the eleven died. They died of blood loss and of shock and, two of them, of the wound going bad a fortnight later in a house with no way of stopping it. Worse than that number is what sits behind it. At least two of the eight were bitten through a coat and a shirt, and there is a real chance neither of them was ever infected. They had a leg taken off in a kitchen on a maybe. Nobody can tell in the first two minutes whether skin was broken, and the first two minutes is the entire window. Raghunathan's own note is the honest one and I will not improve on it. This is a procedure with three survivors and eight graves, and the survivors are the ones who tell you about it.

quote: Take the boring shelf.
what_it_means: By the second year every obvious thing had gone from every shop in this county and the boring shelf was untouched, and it still is.
